stimuli.text: Initial-rate data for A + B → products:
A student heats 11.3 g of $$\ce{CaCO3(s)}$$, which decomposes completely: $$\ce{CaCO3(s) -> CaO(s) + CO2(g)}$$. The $$\ce{CO2}$$ is collected at 298 K and 0.97 atm.
The decomposition of compound X was monitored at constant temperature.
A student titrates 36.0 mL of 0.19 M weak monoprotic acid HA (Ka = 1.4 \times 10^{-4}) with 0.09 M NaOH.
9.8 g of $$\ce{CaCl2}$$ dissolves in 130 g of water in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The temperature rises by 7.2 °C. Assume the solution's specific heat is 4.18 J/(g·°C).

A galvanic cell is made of a Zn electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Zn^{2+}}$$ and a Ni electrode in 1.0 M $$\ce{Ni^{2+}}$$. Standard reduction potentials: $$\ce{Zn^{2+} + 2e- -> Zn}$$ E° = -0.76 V; $$\ce{Ni^{2+} + 2e- -> Ni}$$ E° = -0.25 V.
The photoelectron spectra of C (Z = 6) and N (Z = 7) are compared.

questions.stem: Which bond is the most polar?

options.why: Correct. It has the largest electronegativity difference (1.2).

questions.stem: Why does increasing temperature increase reaction rate?

options.text: A larger fraction of collisions have energy at or above the activation energy

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.05 M solution of $$\ce{NaOH}$$ at 25 °C?

options.why: Strong acids and bases ionize completely; no equilibrium is needed.
Correct. Strong base: [OH⁻] = 1 × 0.05 M; pH = 14 − pOH.
That is the pOH; subtract from 14.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 39.3 g. The actual yield is 22 g. What is the percent yield?
How many formula units or molecules are in 63 g of $$\ce{CaCO3}$$?

options.why: Correct. Convert grams to moles, then multiply by Avogadro's number.

questions.stem: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 38.2 g. The actual yield is 35.5 g. What is the percent yield?
A solution has an absorbance of 0.934 in a 2 cm cuvette. The molar absorptivity is 161 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
Samples of $$\ce{Ar}$$, $$\ce{CO2}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$, $$\ce{N2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.
N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
Ar has a larger molar mass (40 g/mol).
CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).

questions.explanation: Molar masses: Ar 40, CO2 44, H2 2.02, N2 28.

questions.stem: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, $$\ce{MgF2}$$ or $$\ce{KBr}$$?

options.text: $$\ce{KBr}$$, because it has more atoms per formula unit
options.why: Number of atoms does not determine lattice energy.

options.text: $$\ce{MgF2}$$, because its ions have larger charges
options.why: Correct. By Coulomb's law, attraction increases with the product of the ion charges.

options.text: $$\ce{KBr}$$, because its ions have larger charges
They are equal because both are ionic

questions.explanation: MgF2 has ion charges 2 and 1; KBr has 1 and 1.

questions.stem: What volume does 1.07 mol of gas occupy at 0.851 atm and 252 K?

options.why: Use R = 0.08206 with atm and L.
22.4 L/mol applies only at 0 °C and 1 atm.

questions.stem: Under which conditions does a real gas deviate most from ideal behavior?

options.why: Correct. Particle volume and attractions matter most.

questions.explanation: Particle volume and attractions matter most.

questions.stem: Why is solid NaCl a poor conductor while molten NaCl conducts?

options.text: Ions are fixed in the solid but mobile in the liquid

questions.stem: When a salt dissolves in water, the temperature of the solution decreases. Which is true?

options.text: The process is endothermic; energy flows from the water into the dissolving process
The water's molecules gain kinetic energy

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.162 mol of solute in enough water to make 752 mL of solution?
Why is HI a stronger acid than HF?

options.text: The H–I bond is weaker and I⁻ is larger, so H⁺ is released more easily
options.why: Correct. Bond strength decreases down the group.

options.text: F is less electronegative than I

questions.explanation: Bond strength decreases down the group.

questions.stem: A 35.6 mL sample of $$\ce{H2SO4}$$ is titrated to the equivalence point with 17.2 mL of 0.072 M NaOH. What is the concentration of the acid?

options.why: Correct. Each H₂SO₄ reacts with two OH⁻, so divide the moles of NaOH by 2.

questions.stem: 198 g of water at 81 °C is mixed with 186 g of water at 13 °C in an insulated container. What is the final temperature?

options.why: Correct. Heat lost = heat gained; for water alone, a mass-weighted average.
Pair each mass with its own temperature.

questions.stem: A first-order reaction has a rate constant of 0.033 min⁻¹. What is its half-life?
What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 183 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: What is the molarity of a solution made by dissolving 0.084 mol of solute in enough water to make 768 mL of solution?
A gas mixture contains 0.5 mol N₂, 0.2 mol O₂ and 0.4 mol Ar at a total pressure of 1.7 atm. What is the partial pressure of N₂?

options.why: Use the mole fraction, not moles.
The gases are not present in equal amounts.

questions.stem: Which has a larger first ionization energy, Mg or Ba, and why?

options.text: Ba, because it has more protons
options.why: Shielding and distance outweigh the extra protons.

options.text: They are equal because both are in Group 2
Mg, because its valence electrons are closer to the nucleus
options.why: Correct. Down a group, electrons are farther away and more shielded.
Larger atoms lose electrons more easily.

questions.explanation: Down a group, electrons are farther away and more shielded.

questions.stem: A weak acid HA has pKa = 4.1. In a solution at pH 5.5, which statement is correct?

options.why: Correct. Above the pKa, the deprotonated form dominates.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 225 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3}$$, 16 g of $$\ce{Fe}$$ reacts with 26 g of $$\ce{O2}$$. What mass of $$\ce{Fe2O3}$$ can form?

options.why: Apply the mole ratio from the equation.
Use the limiting reactant, which gives less product.
Correct. Fe is the limiting reactant.
Not all of both reactants reacts.

questions.stem: When a reaction involving 0.089 mol of limiting reactant occurs in 196 g of solution (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C)), the temperature rises by 4.8 °C. What is ΔH for the reaction?

options.why: A temperature rise means the reaction is exothermic (negative ΔH).
Correct. q(solution) = mcΔT = 3930 J; q(reaction) = −q(solution); divide by moles.
Divide by the moles of reactant.

questions.stem: What is the oxidation number of N in $$\ce{NO3^-}$$?

options.why: Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.
Correct. The oxidation numbers must sum to the species' overall charge (O usually −2, H usually +1).
Make the oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge.

questions.stem: How many valence electrons are shown in the Lewis structure of $$\ce{PCl3}$$?

options.why: Correct. Sum the valence electrons of all atoms, then add one per negative charge (subtract one per positive charge).

questions.stem: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?

options.text: It provides a pathway with a lower activation energy
options.why: Correct. The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

questions.explanation: The reaction goes by a different mechanism.

questions.stem: What is the hybridization of the central atom in $$\ce{CCl4}$$?

options.why: Count electron domains, including lone pairs.
Correct. Hybridization matches the number of electron domains: 2 sp, 3 sp², 4 sp³.
Count electron domains, including lone pairs.
Count electron domains, including lone pairs.

questions.explanation: CCl4 has 4 electron domains on the central atom.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 1.7 M and [I₂] = 0.7 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 0.78 M. What is K?
Which is a physical change?

options.why: Correct. Only intermolecular forces are overcome.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{2N2O5 -> 4NO2 + O2}$$, $$\ce{N2O5}$$ is consumed at 0.33 M/s. At what rate does $$\ce{NO2}$$ form?

options.why: Correct. Multiply by the coefficient ratio 4/2.
Divide by the reactant's coefficient too.

questions.stem: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH negative, which change shifts the equilibrium toward NH₃?

options.why: Correct. The product side has fewer moles of gas.
The reaction is exothermic; heating shifts left.

questions.explanation: The product side has fewer moles of gas.

questions.stem: For $$\ce{A(g) + B(g) <=> 2C(g)}$$, K = 8.2. A mixture has [A] = 0.6 M, [B] = 0.3 M and [C] = 0.7 M. In which direction will the reaction proceed?

options.text: It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 3.89
It is at equilibrium, because Q = K
It proceeds forward, toward products, because Q = 2.72
options.why: Correct. Q = [C]²/([A][B]) = 2.72, which is less than K.

options.text: It proceeds in reverse, toward reactants, because Q = 2.72
options.why: If Q is less than K, the reaction proceeds forward.

questions.stem: Samples of $$\ce{Cl2}$$, $$\ce{CO2}$$, $$\ce{N2}$$, $$\ce{H2}$$ are all at the same temperature. Which has the highest average molecular speed?

options.why: Cl2 has a larger molar mass (70.9 g/mol).
CO2 has a larger molar mass (44 g/mol).
N2 has a larger molar mass (28 g/mol).
Correct. At the same temperature, average kinetic energy is equal, so the lightest gas moves fastest.

questions.explanation: Molar masses: Cl2 70.9, CO2 44, N2 28, H2 2.02.

questions.stem: How many moles of gas are in a 20 L flask at 2.67 atm and 318 K?
A weak acid (pKa 4.74) is titrated with NaOH; the equivalence point is reached at 39 mL. What is the pH after 19.5 mL of NaOH has been added?

options.why: Correct. At the half-equivalence point, [HA] = [A⁻], so pH = pKa.
That is only for strong acid–strong base equivalence.

questions.stem: A reaction has K = 34. What is K for the reaction multiplied by ½?

options.why: Correct. Reverse → 1/K; multiply by n → Kⁿ.
Multiplying by n raises K to the nth power.
K is raised to a power, not multiplied.

questions.stem: On a reaction energy profile, the reactants are at 84 kJ/mol, the transition state at 136 kJ/mol and the products at 109 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the reverse reaction?

options.why: Measure from the correct starting point.
Correct. Reverse Ea = transition state − products.

questions.explanation: Forward Ea = 52, ΔH = 25, reverse Ea = 27 kJ/mol.

questions.stem: What is the mass percent of H in $$\ce{H2SO4}$$?

options.why: That is the percent of the other elements.
Use masses, not numbers of atoms.
There are 2 atoms of H in the formula.

questions.stem: What is the rate law?

options.why: Orders are found from the data, not from coefficients.
Recheck how the rate changes when [B] doubles.
Correct. Doubling [A] multiplies the rate by 4; doubling [B] multiplies it by 2.
Compare trials where only one concentration changes.

questions.explanation: Trials 1→2: rate ×4, so order 2 in A. Trials 1→3: rate ×2, so order 1 in B.

questions.stem: Which is the ground-state electron configuration of selenium (Se, Z = 34)?

options.why: Correct. Fill orbitals in order until 34 electrons are placed.

questions.stem: What is the energy of a photon with a wavelength of 629 nm?

options.why: Correct. E = hc/λ, with λ in meters.

questions.stem: In a Zn/Cu galvanic cell, [Zn²⁺] is increased. What happens to the cell potential?

options.why: Correct. A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.explanation: A product's concentration rises, so Q increases.

questions.stem: At 298 K, ΔG° for a reaction is 14 kJ/mol. What is K?

options.why: Correct. K = e^(−ΔG°/RT), with ΔG° in J/mol and R = 8.314.

questions.explanation: ln K = -5.65; K = 3.52 \times 10^{-3}. Positive ΔG°: K less than 1.

questions.stem: What is the pH of a 0.1 M solution of nitrous acid (Ka = 4.5 \times 10^{-4})?

options.why: A weak acid does not ionize completely.
Correct. Solve Ka = x²/(C − x) for x = [H₃O⁺].

questions.stem: What is E°cell for a galvanic cell made from these half-cells?

options.why: E° does not change when half-reactions are multiplied.
Cathode minus anode; a galvanic cell is positive.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.13 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 9.25) and 0.41 mol of A⁻. What is its pH?
For a reaction, ΔH° = -55 kJ/mol and ΔS° = 185 J/(mol·K). What is ΔG° at 349 K, and is the reaction favorable?

options.why: Convert ΔS from J to kJ.
Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, with ΔS in kJ/(mol·K).

questions.stem: A photoelectron spectrum shows 5 peaks. From highest to lowest binding energy, their relative heights are 2 : 2 : 6 : 2 : 1. Which element is it?

options.why: Correct. The peaks correspond to $$1s^{2}\,2s^{2}\,2p^{6}\,3s^{2}\,3p^{1}$$, which has 13 electrons.

questions.stem: Calculate ΔH° for $$\ce{2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3}$$. (ΔH°f of O₂ is 0.)

options.why: Multiply each ΔH°f by its coefficient.
Correct. Σ n ΔH°f(products) − Σ n ΔH°f(reactants).

questions.stem: For $$\ce{H2(g) + I2(g) <=> 2HI(g)}$$, initial [H₂] = 2 M and [I₂] = 1.7 M, with no HI. At equilibrium, [HI] = 1.54 M. What is K?
The Ksp of $$\ce{AgBr}$$ is 5 \times 10^{-13}. What is its molar solubility in pure water?

options.why: This salt gives two ions: Ksp = s².

questions.stem: The first four ionization energies of an element are 792, 1489, 10423, 15009 kJ/mol. In which group of the periodic table is the element most likely found?

options.why: Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.
Correct. The large jump comes after removing 2 electrons, so it has 2 valence electrons.
Locate the largest jump between successive ionization energies.

questions.explanation: The big jump marks the start of removing core electrons.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.26 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 9.25) and 0.27 mol of its conjugate base A⁻. Then 0.06 mol of HCl is added. What is the pH?

options.why: Correct. First react: H⁺ converts A⁻ to HA. Then pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
Update moles after the added acid or base reacts.

questions.stem: Reaction 1 has ΔH₁ = -151 kJ and reaction 2 has ΔH₂ = -42 kJ. A target reaction is obtained by doubling reaction 1 and adding reaction 2. What is ΔH for the target reaction?

options.why: Reversing changes the sign of ΔH₂.
Correct. Reverse → change sign; multiply → multiply ΔH; then add.
Enthalpies add; they do not multiply.

questions.stem: A buffer contains 0.1 mol of a weak acid HA (pKa 4.2) and 0.14 mol of its conjugate base A⁻. Then 0.04 mol of HCl is added. What is the pH?

options.why: Correct. First react: H⁺ converts A⁻ to HA. Then pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).

questions.stem: Use the bond enthalpies to estimate ΔH for $$\ce{H2 + Br2 -> 2HBr}$$.

options.why: Broken minus formed, not formed minus broken.
Multiply each bond energy by the number of bonds.
Correct. ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Bonds formed release energy: subtract them.

questions.stem: What is E°cell for a galvanic cell made from these half-cells?

options.why: Cathode minus anode; a galvanic cell is positive.
E° does not change when half-reactions are multiplied.

parts.prompt: Calculate the number of moles of CO₂ produced.

rubric.criterion: Correct moles using molar mass 100.09 g/mol and the 1:1 ratio.

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of CO₂ expected.
The student measures 2.476 L of gas. Calculate the percent yield, and give one experimental reason the yield could be less than 100%.

rubric.example: Incomplete decomposition (not heated long enough) or gas leaking from the apparatus.

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a complete Lewis diagram for CO₂, and identify its molecular geometry and the hybridization of carbon.

rubric.example: O=C=O with two lone pairs on each O (16 valence electrons).

parts.prompt: Explain why CO₂ is nonpolar even though C=O bonds are polar.

rubric.criterion: Linear symmetry makes the bond dipoles cancel.

parts.prompt: CaO is an ionic solid. Explain, using Coulomb's law, why CaO has a higher melting point than KCl.

rubric.criterion: Larger ion charges in CaO (2+/2−) than in KCl (1+/1−).
Greater electrostatic attraction (and smaller ions) means more energy is needed to separate the ions.

parts.prompt: Calculate the average rate of disappearance of X between 0 and 20 s.
Determine the order of the reaction with respect to X. Justify your answer using the data.

rubric.example: Equal time intervals give equal changes in ln[X].

parts.prompt: Write the rate law and determine the rate constant, with units.
Calculate the half-life of the reaction (for the initial concentration).
A proposed mechanism has a slow first step: X → Y + Z. Is the mechanism consistent with the rate law? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Yes; the slow step's elementary rate law matches the observed rate law.

parts.prompt: A catalyst is added. Explain its effect on the rate and on the rate constant, using activation energy.

rubric.example: The catalyst provides a new pathway.

rubric.criterion: Lower activation energy means a larger fraction of collisions are successful.

parts.prompt: Write the net ionic equation for the titration reaction.
Calculate the initial pH of the acid solution.

rubric.criterion: Ka expression set up with x = [H₃O⁺].

parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH needed to reach the equivalence point.
What is the pH at the half-equivalence point? Justify.
Calculate the pH at the equivalence point.

rubric.criterion: Uses Kb = Kw/Ka and the diluted [A⁻].

parts.prompt: Choose an appropriate indicator from: methyl orange (pKa 3.7), bromothymol blue (pKa 7.0), phenolphthalein (pKa 9.3). Justify.

rubric.criterion: Indicator whose pKa is closest to the equivalence pH.

parts.prompt: Explain why the solution at the half-equivalence point resists pH change when a small amount of HCl is added.

rubric.criterion: A⁻ reacts with added H⁺ to form HA (buffer).
rubric.example: A⁻ + H₃O⁺ → HA + H₂O, so the ratio [A⁻]/[HA] changes only slightly.

parts.prompt: Is the dissolution endothermic or exothermic? Justify.

rubric.example: Exothermic: the solution warmed, so energy was released.

parts.prompt: Calculate the heat absorbed or released by the solution.
Calculate ΔH of dissolution in kJ/mol.
If some heat escaped to the surroundings, would the magnitude of the calculated ΔH be too large or too small? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Too small, because the measured temperature change is smaller than the true change.

parts.prompt: Write the balanced net ionic equation for the cell reaction.
Calculate E°cell.
Calculate ΔG° for the cell reaction.
The concentration of Zn²⁺ is increased to 2.0 M. Predict the effect on the cell potential and justify.

rubric.criterion: E decreases because Q increases (a product's concentration rises).
rubric.example: Q greater than 1 → E less than E°.

questions.title: Solubility of a slightly soluble salt

parts.prompt: Write the Ksp expression.
Calculate the molar solubility in pure water.
Calculate the molar solubility in a solution containing 0.05 M I⁻ (from a soluble salt).
Would lowering the pH significantly change the solubility? Explain.

rubric.criterion: Correct reasoning about whether the anion is basic.
rubric.example: No: I⁻ is the conjugate base of a strong acid, so H⁺ does not remove it.

parts.prompt: Write the electron configuration of N.
Explain why the 1s peak of N has a higher binding energy than the 1s peak of C.

rubric.criterion: N has more protons, so 1s electrons are attracted more strongly (Coulomb's law).

parts.prompt: Describe one difference in the number or relative height of peaks between the two spectra.

rubric.criterion: A valid difference based on configurations.
rubric.example: N has one more electron, so its outermost peak is taller or an extra peak appears.

parts.prompt: Which element has the larger atomic radius? Justify using Coulomb's law.

rubric.criterion: C: fewer protons with similar shielding, so valence electrons are held less tightly.
rubric.example: Same period; effective nuclear charge increases across.
